speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: RESIGNATION OF HON. P. J. A. CARDIN-TABLING OF CORRESPONDENCE
speechtext:
I regret to inform the house of the resignation to-day of the Hon. Mr. Cardin as a minister of the crown. The cir-
cumstances of Mr. Cardin's resignation and of its acceptance by His Excellency the Governor General will appear from the following correspondence.
On Saturday afternoon, Mr. Cardin personally handed to me the following communication: Office of the Minister of Public Works Ottawa, May 9, 1942. My dear Prime Minister,
As a result of the decision arrived at during the meeting of council yesterday, where I once more expressed my point of view and my reasons for not agreeing with the new policy of the government, I respectfully tender my resignation as Minister of Public Works and Minister of Transport.
I feel that there is no necessity for repeating here the arguments which, I sincerely believe, justify my action. Suffice it to say at present that, as far as Canada is concerned, since the question of the plebiscite was first discussed and since the vote has been taken, nothing has been said nor anything established to indicate that the war situation has rendered necessary, just a few days after the vote, the introduction of a measure containing the principle of compulsory military service for overseas.
The presentation at this time, of an amendment to abrogate clause 3 of the National Mobilization Act is not, in my judgment, in accordance with the attitude taken and the views expressed in the speeches and declarations made soliciting an affirmative vote on the plebiscite.
I desire to express, my dear Prime Minister, my deep appreciation of your personal consideration, goodwill and friendship.
Most sincerely yours,
P. J. Arthur Cardin
The Right Honourable W. L. Mackenzie King, Prime Minister,
Ottawa.
To Mr. Cardin's letter I made the following reply:
Office of the Prime Minister
Ottawa, May 11, 1942.
My dear Cardin,
In your letter of the 9th instant, which you so kindly handed to me personally, you state that you are tendering your resignation on the ground that you are unable to agree with the new policy of the government. You also give certain arguments which you feel justify your action.
Had the government adopted a new policy, a policy with which you ivere unable to agree, I could take no exception to your tendering your resignation. Indeed, it would be the only right and proper course for you to take. There has, however, been no change of policy. No new policy has been adopted.
The decision of the cabinet to seek from parliament an amendment to the National Resources Mobilization Act, deleting clause 3 of the act, does not denote any change in government policy. The sole purpose of the proposed amendment is to obtain for the government the freedom of decision and action with respect to the method of raising men for

The Ministry-Hon. P. J. A. Cardin
military service overseas which, in the recent plebiscite, the government itself requested, and which, by a very large majority, the people of Canada have said they desire the government to possess.
The statutory restriction contained in section 3 is the one remaining restriction on the government's freedom of decision and action in all aspects of Canada's war effort. The section was included in the National Resources Mobilization Act at the time the bill was before parliament because of a commitment arising out of promises and pledges from which the government and members of parliament have been released by the results of the recent plebiscite.
As you are aware, the government might have proceeded in this matter by order in council under the War Measures Act. Having regard, however, to its responsibility to parliament, the government has felt that such action as is necessary to bring existing legislation into conformity with the will of the people expressed in the vote on the plebiscite should be taken, not by order in council under the War Measures Act, but by act of parliament. In thus proceeding, the government is, before any amendment to the National Resources Mobilization Act is made, providing members of parliament with the fullest opportunity of considering the effect of every aspect of the amendment.
You will recall that, in my broadcasts, I stressed the fact that, despite the magnificence of Canada's war effort, the quite unfounded impression was being fostered in our own country and among other nations that, because of a restriction upon the powers of the government, Canada's effort was not, and could never be an all-out effort.
I gave the strongest reasons why this false impression, and the injustice being done Canada in the eyes of our own people and in the eyes of the world, should be ended as speedily as possible. In those reasons and in the fact that already it is desirable to extend the scope of service under the National Resources Mobilization Act to other parts of this continent and adjacent islands, you will find, I believe, wherein the war situation has rendered necessary the introduction, without delay, of the proposed amendment to the National Resources Mobilization Act.
In view of the grounds on which you have tendered your resignation, I cannot but feel that you have given to the decision of the government a significance it was never intended to have. I therefore feel that before taking any action on your letter, I should place before you, anew, the situation as I see it. You may feel that, in the light of what I have said, you would care to reconsider the request of your letter. I shall gladly await any further consideration you may wish to give the matter.
With kindest personal regards,
Yours very sincerely,
W. L. Mackenzie King The Honourable P. J. A. Cardin, M.P.,
Minister of Public Works,
Ottawa.
The letter I have just read was delivered to Mr. Cardin this morning. Shortly thereafter I received from Mr. Cardin the following reply:
Office of the Minister of Public Works
Ottawa, May 11, 1942.
My dear Prime Minister:
Your communication of this morning with reference to my resignation reached me but a short time ago, and is one more indication of your kindness to me and of your friendship, which I greatly appreciate and thank you for most sincerely.
On perusing the letter, I find, however, that it merely presents anew the arguments, interpretations and viewpoints put forward during the discussion which preceded the decision arrived at in council, on Friday last.
I regret, therefore, my inability to change the views conveyed to you in the letter which I personally handed you on Saturday afternoon.
With the expression of my warmest personal regards, I am, my dear Prime Minister,
Yours very sincerely,
P. J. Arthur Cardin
The Right Honourable W. L. Mackenzie King, Prime Minister,
Ottawa.
On receiving Mr. Cardin's letter I sent to him the following reply:
Office of the Prime Minister,
Canada
Ottawa, May 11, 1942.
My dear Cardin:
It is with great regret that I have learned of your decision not to withdraw the tender of your resignation. In the circumstances, I have had no alternative but to inform the governor general of the correspondence which has passed between us, and to advise his excellency to accept your resignation. I have now to let you know that your resignation, as a minister of the crown, has been accepted by his excellency.
Since the passing of Lapointe and Dandurand, you have been, in years of association, my oldest colleague in the cabinet. We have been together in parliament for many years. For thirteen of these years we have shared the responsibilities of office. Over all these years, our political and personal associations have been so close and so friendly that the severance of the relationship which your retirement from the government involves, means, I can assure you, not less to myself than I know it does to you.
I thank you for the words of appreciation and personal friendship conveyed in your letteT. They are most warmly reciprocated by myself. I wish to thank you in equal measure for your unfailing loyalty and constant and helpful cooperation in the work of the administration, during the years we have shared its tasks together.

The Plebiscite

May I express the hope that release from the responsibilities and anxieties of office which are so very great at this most critical of all times, may serve further to restore your health and strength from the impairment it suffered some months ago, from which, fortunately, you have steadily recovered.
With renewed expressions of my warmest personal regards and with my best wishes,
Believe me, my dear Cardin,
Yours very sincerely,
W. L. Mackenzie King The Honourable P. J. A. Cardin, M.P.,
Minister of Public Works,
Ottawa.

subtopic: STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER AS TO RESULT OF VOTE

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER AS TO RESULT OF VOTE
speechtext:
The results of the plebiscite on April 27 are now all but complete. Although final official returns are not yet available, the most reliable figures indicate that on the question asked there were over 2,926,856 persons who voted in the affirmative, and over 1,618,730 persons who voted in the negative; in other words 64 per cent of the voters answered in the affirmative and 36 per cent in the negative.
The total number of votes cast on the plebiscite is an impressive demonstration of the importance which the electors of Canada attach to giving to the government a free hand at a time of war.
The question on which the people of Canada were asked to express an opinion was:
Are you in favour of releasing the government from any obligation arising out of any past commitments restricting the methods of raising men for military service?
By their vote, the people have decisively expressed the view that the government should be released from any such obligation. In other words, there no longer remains any issue which the government or members of parliament, because of past promises or pledges are restricted from considering, dis-
cussing and deciding on its merits, in the light of what is best for Canada and for Canada's war effort.
The question in the plebiscite was of equal concern to all citizens of Canada. The result is a national expression of view on a national issue. It should be so viewed in all its aspects. In all of the provinces, and for that matter, in every constituency, affirmative and negative votes were cast. The vote was taken in a democratic fashion. It will be recognized throughout the country that, in a democracy, the will of the majority should prevail.
The vote in the plebiscite shows that the people generally recognize that the war has taken a course which was altogether unforeseen; that conditions wholly unexpected may yet arise, and that, in consequence, there should be no restriction upon the freedom of the government apart from its constitutional responsibility to parliament.
In the plebiscite, the electors were not called upon to vote for or against the government. The result, therefore, is not to be construed as a vote for any political party. In fact, the plebiscite was selected by the government precisely because it afforded the best known means of obtaining an expression of the views of the people on a specific question, regardless of political parties, or party considerations.
As, in'some quarters, an effort has been made since the plebiscite to interpret the result as a mandate for conscription for overseas service, it is necessary for me to repeat that, in the plebiscite, conscription was not the issue. The government did not ask the people to say whether or not conscription for overseas service should be adopted. That was not the issue before the people. With respect to the issue of conscription, the result can only rightly be construed as leaving to the government and to parliament entire freedom to deal with that question on its merits.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
the purpose of the amendment is to give to the government, by the deletion of section 3 of the National Resources Mobilization Act, the same freedom of decision and action with respect to the method of raising men for military services overseas which, in the recent plebiscite the government requested, and) which the people of Canada have said they desire the government to possess.
Section 3 ^contains the one remaining restriction on the'government's freedom of decision and action in all aspects of Canada's war effort.
This section was included in the National Resources Mobilization Act, at the time the bill was passed, because of a commitment arising out of promises and pledges from which the government and members of parliament have now been released.
In presenting the issue of the plebiscite to parliament and to the people, I repeatedly stressed the importance of removing any restriction, or even the appearance of any restriction, on the powers of the government to effect a total effort for total war. I pointed out that Canada's war effort was being placed in a false light because of the existence of what appears to be a restriction upon an all-out effort. If the amendment is adopted, Canada's war effort will appear thereafter in its true light; an effort in no way hampered by any moral or legal restrictions. By their vote in the plebiscite, the people have expressed their readiness to have the sole remaining restriction upon the government's freedom and decision of action removed.
The removal of section 3 of the National Resources Mobilization Act is, in other words, the logical consequence of the vote on the plebiscite. Since the people have indicated that they do not desire any restriction on the freedom of action of the government, there is

the strongest of reasons why parliament should be asked to remove any shadow of restriction which remains.
In the plebiscite, the people were asked to give full powers to the government, not to meet a then immediate situation, but to provide against a future emergency. The National Resources Mobilization Act is only enabling legislation. The extent of the use of such power as is conferred upon the government by its provisions is and has, from the outset, been a matter of government policy, to be decided in the light of all relevant circumstances. This will remain true of the unrestricted powers which the amendment, if enacted, would afford.
The government might have proceeded in this matter by order in council under the War Measures Act. Having regard, however, to its responsibility to parliament, the government has felt that such action as is necessary to bring existing legislation into conformity with the will of the people expressed in the vote on the plebiscite should be taken, not by order in council under the War Measures Act, but by act of parliament. In thus proceeding, the government is providing members of parliament, before any amendment to the National Resources Mobilization Act is made, with the fullest opportunity of considering the effect of every aspect of the amendment.

Would the minister explain the nature of the naval developments which I understand have been taking place on Grand lake, Nova Scotia, and

War Appropriation-Naval Services
why a fresh water lake, the largest in Nova Scotia it is true, is being used? Also can the minister give any further particulars as to the naval college which was definitely announced on Thursday or Friday as being established in British Columbia? Why was this college removed from Nova Scotia, and what naval instruction is it proposed to carry on in Nova Scotia? It is with some regret that the people of Nova Scotia see the naval college which was located for a considerable time in that province being removed. It is one of the unfortunate developments that a great deal of the war activities operating in Nova Scotia are only temporary and will cease at the termination of the war. Very little is being developed there which will have a survival value. The naval college was one of the departmental activities that is not only necessary at the present time but should continue after the war as a permanent institution.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
The Grand Lake development is a matter which has not yet been decided on affirmatively. There may be no development there. If there were it would be in the nature of a school for the training of men in signalling, which could be carried on quite conveniently at Grand Lake.
As to the naval college, the decision has been made to re-establish it at or near Esquimalt, British Columbia. It is true the college was established in Halifax at the beginning. It was destroyed in the great explosion, set up again for a time at Kingston as part of the Royal Military College, and finally at Esquimalt until it was closed in 1923. After very careful thought the decision was reached that, all in all, Esquimalt offered unusual opportunities. The property there, one square mile in area, was acquired at a very reasonable rate; it contains a very fine building already, and it was felt that on account of the favourable western climate the college would be better established there where year-round training in boat work can be had.

I appreciate
the minister's explanation. The intention appears to be definite to reestablish this naval college on the Pacific coast. Nova Scotia, however, does not willingly relinquish its claim to the location of this college. By the removal of the college the prestige of the province as the centre of naval activities and naval developments is diminished. The people of the province feel that they have certaip rights in the matter, and the opinion is definitely held there, and I believe it is shared in other parts of Canada, that Nova Scotia is the proper location in that it is in
closer contact with the mother country and with the development of naval service in Great Britain in conjunction with what is or may be done in that regard in Canada. It is believed that the Atlantic coast is a more appropriate location for the college so that it might operate in conjunction with the British naval authorities. It was unfortunate that the old college was destroyed in the explosion, but the province should not suffer on that account. I do not question the attractiveness of the location on the Pacific coast, but speaking for Nova Scotia I do not yield the claims of that province to location and reestablishment of the college on the Atlantic coast. As I say, it is unfortunate that so much of the development in Nova Scotia that has arisen out of the war, such as transportation by water and by rail, and work in the coal mines, and other activities, will cease on the termination of hostilities, which we hope will not be long delayed. We feel that a permanent asset or institution such as the naval college should not lightly be taken away from Nova Scotia.
Mr. MACDONALD (Kingston City); All I can say to my hon. friend is that I hope there will be laid next week in Nova Scotia the keels of two destroyers, the first time that the building of ships of war of that size have ever been undertaken in this country. If there is to be a navy at all in Canada after the war, as I hope there always will be, destroyers will form a necessary part of it, and the natural and proper place to build them, at least a very suitable place, I think, is in Nova Scotia. The building of destroyers is from the point of view of the province a much more desirable thing than the establishment of a college. After all the college will contain no more than 100 students at any one time, fifty a year coming in. It is about the same as if fifty more students were added to the enrolment of Dalhousie or Acadia, or any of the maritime universities. ' I do not think that is to be compared to the prospect of a permanent destroyer-building programme in Nova Scotia.

Is there not considerable
naval training going on at Halifax with King's college as a base, and are there not also many young Canadians who have been instructed as officers in the Canadian navy there?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Yes, there is training going on at King's, and there has been training for officers going on at other points since the beginning of the war. That is a shorter course, covering four months. We are speaking now of the college, which has a two-year course.

War Appropriation-Naval Services

Would the minister explain the requirements for entry to this new naval college, and also the age standards that have been set? We have had some complaints to the effect that the age limit is so low that young lads in some of the provinces cannot matriculate in time to qualify for the college, and it is felt that the result may be that boys from these provinces never will get into the college.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I do not think there is anything in that. There has been some complaint from British Columbia that the age limit is not satisfactory to them, but it is impossible to get exact equality of educational training in all the provinces. It is impossible to find students reaching the same point in their educational progress at exactly the same time. I think the superintendent of education in British Columbia made some complaint, but he was interviewed by the naval director of education and it was explained to him that we did not believe that any bright boy in British Columbia would be handicapped as a result of the age limit. Taking July 1, 1942, as the vital date, the requirement is that a boy must be over sixteen and not more than seventeen years and eight months as of that date, and he must have what is commonly called junior matriculation in order to enter. That is the general standard of admission. For the first year, that is for this year, we are making an exception, however. Boys can enter for one year only, taking a one-year course, who are beyond those age limits. They may enter even if they are up to the age of nineteen, I think, or perhaps it is eighteen years and eight months. In the paymaster branch they may enter up to twenty. But the standard age for entry will be over sixteen and under seventeen years and eight months. That has been arrived at after consultation with the departments of education of the nine provinces, and it is felt to be a reasonably fair and proper age limit to set.

Would it not be possible to make some special allowance in a case where the provincial educational regulations make it impossible for a boy to be that far ahead at that age? They are very strict in British Columbia in not allowing a youngster, no matter how bright he may be, to skip grades; and the result may be that it will be almost impossible for a young chap from that province to get into the naval college.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Well, I do not know. Are there many bright boys-

I am only talking of bright boys; we are not interested in the dullards, because there would be no reason for their going there-
I hope the minister does not mean to suggest that there are no bright boys in British Columbia.
That is another reason why the college should be located in Nova Scotia; they are all bright there.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Will there be any bright boy in British Columbia who will not have received his junior matriculation by the age of seventeen years and eight months? I should think nearly all these boys would be that far on. I am given to understand that the number of those who might be hampered or prevented from entering the college as a result of the age limit would be very small.

I am told that under our school regulations it is almost impossible for a boy to be that far along at that age. I would ask the minister to look into the situation again and, if he finds it impossible for a boy from British Columbia to get into the college under the present regulations, some special allowance should be made, because it is not the fault of the boy.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: My hon. friend may rest assured that we will do right by British Columbia.

I believe the regulations concerning the Royal Military college provide that a certain number of students shall be allotted to each province. Are there any such regulations in respect to the new naval college?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes, there is provision to the effect that we shall try to divide the number of students among the provinces, in proportion to the number of applications coming from the provinces.

High school students in British Columbia are required to take a four-year course. That does result in some of them getting through a little later; but the correspondence referred to by the minister, with the superintendent of education, will show that the percentage of boys who are not through at the required age is very small, and in conversation with myself the superintendent stated that this really was not a serious point.
With reference to the question of the location of the college I have a suggestion to offer. I know that the hon. member for Cumberland is a very reasonable gentleman, as

War Appropriation-Naval Services
are most people who come from that wonderful province. I would invite him to come to Victoria and let us show him the new Royal Roads college. If, after he has visited the place and has seen the kind of deal the government were able to make, he is not quite satisfied that the minister did the right thing in selecting that site for the college, we will have to do something very handsome for him. I am sure, however, that nowhere else in Canada could he find surroundings equal to those at Royal Roads, and that nowhere else could the government have obtained for a very few thousand dollars property valued at something over a million. It is an excellent location, close to the Esquimalt harbour and with year-round facilities, and I am sure that after he has seen the place the hon. member will be satisfied that the minister made the proper choice.

Ha? the minister considered the possibility of this country having a seaman's manual of its own, instead of the out-dated manuals the boys have to use at the present time? They are now using volume 1, 1937, and volume 2, 1938, and these volumes are unrevised. In the United States the navy department is issuing "Knight's Modern Seamanship", which is revised right up to March, 1942. That manual is right up to date: it covers everything, oil burners, depth charges, torpedoes, bombs, up-to-date anti-aircraft guns, and everything else. The manual we are using in Canada is the one issued by the British admiralty, and it is dull. A moment ago the minister was speaking of bright boys, but even bright boys find that manual dull, and I believe the Canadian navy should have a manual of its own. [DOT]
While I am on my feet I should like to say something else. If a boy wants to join the navy and he lives in the Stratford district, for example, he has to go to London to enlist. They tell him there that they are full up, and he will have to wait. In Hamilton or Toronto, however, the quotas may not be filled. Could not the navy look after that boy, instead of making him wait perhaps months before he is permitted to enlist?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It is true that the seamanship manual used is the manual of 1937, as prepared by the British admiralty. It is not up to date, but after all is said and done we have turned out some pretty good seamen with this manual.

I
acknowledge that.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
While other manuals may be a little more modern
or more interesting, I think our manual still is good. However, I shall be glad to look into the point, and I thank my hon. friend for having raised it. As to the second point, it is true that the navy does its recruiting through these volunteer reserve divisions. The nearest to Stratford would be the one at London, and it is quite possible that boys seeking enlistment at London might find the complement there filled. I think that is very likely to happen. The complement everywhere is filled-in fact more than filled. There are some four to five thousand young men throughout Canada waiting to get into the navy. Some of those young men are no doubt in Stratford, some in Toronto, some in Halifax and others at centres of considerable size throughout the country. If a man has special aptitude in a trade, or anything of that sort, I am sure he would instantly be taken in. If he were not taken at London his name would be sent to headquarters and he would be drafted into the navy at once. However, I shall pass on my hon. friend's suggestions to the proper officers.

I understood the minister to say fifty students a year would be taken into the naval college at Victoria when it is in operation. On what basis does he arrive at that number? Does he consider that that is all who will be required by the navy? Since the beginning of the war the navy has been greatly expanded, and there is still a great deal of expansion going on. Fifty a year seems a small number of students if we are to have any sort of navy.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: We will not rely on the college for the great body of our officers-not at all. We will continue the training of officers at Halifax and at Esquimalt for the four months period under which they now undergo training.
Through the Royal Canadian Naval Volunteer Reserve?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Yes. The college will be for the younger lads between sixteen years and seventeen years eight months. That will go on after as well as during the war. But even after the college is established, the vast majority of officers will come in the way they come to-day, namely through one of these divisions. They will receive a short period of training there, then four months' training at the coast, and then they will be sent to sea for further experience. That is the main source from which we will continue to get our officers during the war. After the war the naval college will form an excellent training ground

War Appropriation-Naval Services
for young men who wish to make their careers in the navy or who wish to enter the merchant marine. Then, it may be used by young men who have no desire for life in either the navy or the merchant marine, but who may wish, or whose parents may wish them, to have the benefit of the discipline and the instruction given by the naval college. I believe it will be of invaluable assistance not only to the navy but to the merchant marine, and to our people as a whole. The training given at the college will be excellent in every way, because we have a splendid staff of instructors. The traditions of the Royal Canadian Navy, following those of the Royal Navy, are high. It would be classed with the Royal Military college at Kingston, which we have had for many years.
What rank would a young man have when taken on in the navy after graduating from the school?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: He would have to start at the bottom of the ladder. He would be a cadet, then a midshipman and then a sub-lieutenant.

Leaving the college he would be a sub-lieutenant, just as in earlier years he would be a sub-lieutenant upon leaving the training cruiser. I believe the college is a substitute, is it not? The young man enters as a cadet, does his work as midshipman, and qualifies at the college to go out as a sub-lieutenant.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I
believe it is probably something like that, although I should not like to speak without the prospectus before me. I am not sure whether he comes out as a cadet or as a sublieutenant. Some would come out when they have barely reached the age of eighteen. Those who go in at sixteen would probably be out a few months before they were eighteen. Then they have to do a year's cadet training. Certainly the rank of sub-lieutenant would be the highest they could possibly hope for on leaving the college.

I have heard it stated that although corvettes are thoroughly seaworthy, in the case of one corvette, owing to the fact that the hatches did not fit properly, water got down into the hold, and there was constantly a foot of water in the room in which the men slept. Secondly, I believe it is a regulation that after six months of service a man is given leave. Is it a fact that after two years some have not been able to get leave to go home, and does that condition arise from lack of men to fill their places?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I
shall look into the first point respecting the corvette. Of course water may get into these ships in various ways, but I should doubt the correctness of the report that the condition arose because the hatch did not fit closely. However I shall look into the matter and find out if there is anything in it.
As to the second question, leave in the navy is usually given to officers and men when the ship comes to a Canadian port for refitting. That is a suitable time, because the ship is laid up anyway, and the officers and men are usually given leave at such times. I know of no cases where men have been at sea for two years without leave. There may have been men living in Toronto or Montreal at the beginning of the war who, perhaps, served a year or so at Halifax and then some further time at sea. But I doubt if there are any cases where a man has been constantly at sea for two years, without leave. However I shall look into the situation, and get the information for the hon. member.

The men in question have not been continuously at sea during that period. We will say that their base is Newfoundland, and that they proceed from there to Iceland, or wherever they are bound to go. On returning to their base for refitting they would have shore leave, of course; but do they have the opportunity of going from their base to their homes in St. John, Halifax, Montreal or wherever they may live? I understand certain of the men have not had that privilege for two years.
Mr.- MACDONALD (Kingston City):	I
am sorry if that is so. I shall make inquiries and give my hon. friend the information.

Overlooking the naval station at Sydney, Nova Scotia, there is a group of five houses which were purchased some two years ago by the Department of Transport. Last year there was some trouble, because the people were ordered out. Eviction notices were served, but there was no place for the occupants of these houses to go. The housing situation in Sydney is deplorable. Last year I succeeded in having the matter straightened out, with the aid of the Minister of Transport. But a new order was issued some three weeks ago and I understand that the naval authorities now desire the removal of these buildings. There are five families affected, thirty people in all. During the last two weeks I have had several letters from different persons in the city, including the mayor, pointing out that there is no room to be had in the city.

War Appropriation-Naval Services
During the past week or so I have taken the matter up with the Department of Transport, but I have had no success in getting a reply. I wonder if the minister would see what can be done with respect to leaving matters as they are until such time as room can be found for the people affected.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I thought there were only three families, but my hon. friend says there are five. These houses are located on a bank overlooking the naval buildings at Sydney.
That is right.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I
understand the occupants of these houses have been in there for some years and I do not think they have ever paid much rent.

Not since the Department
of Transport took over.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The houses are old, and because of their position with regard to the naval buildings, sewage and other drainage I understand seeps down into the cellars of the buildings. I think it is very desirable that these houses should be torn down. I do not know just how I can help my hon. friend. What does he suggest? I know it is hard to get houses in Sydney and I know the city authorities are reluctant to evict people at this time, and have been for some years, because of the housing shortage. If any reasonable method can be found of meeting the situation in order not to inconvenience unduly these poor people-I understand they went in there more or less as squatters-I shall be glad to consider it.

The minister is not correct when he says that they more or less squatted there; they have occupied these houses for years. After the establishment of the naval station, the Department of Transport bought them. There is one thing the minister could do: he could intercede with the Department of Munitions and Supply to consider a prefabricated housing scheme for that city. So far as the city is concerned, they have been trying it for the past two years. Many houses might be made available in that way. As the mayor points out in his letter, if these people are evicted there is no place for them to go except on the street. Last year the Minister of Transport stayed execution, but I notice it is a new magistrate handling this matter this time. Evidently the chap who handled it last year would not tackle it again. The Minister of Transport made an offer last year to the city that if the city would provide land he was prepared to give the buildings
as they were to the city which could move them to the new locations. The mayor's letter is an S.O.S. for a stay of execution until such time as they can find other quarters.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Does the mayor suggest anything that could be done?
No.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is the usual type of letter; they suggest that everything should be done by Ottawa. Let the Department of Transport do it, or the Department of Naval Services. I am not referring particularly to Sydney, but many of these cities are very poor at helping themselves or their own people.
Good at passing the buck.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Exactly, passing the buck. The problem is really one for the city. As I understand it, these people are not war workers, and surely the city of Sydney has some degree of responsibility for its own citizens. Every city expects the government to build houses, to put in water mains and sewers and to provide all sorts of facilities and conveniences, disregarding entirely the fact that they themselves are enjoying a fair amount of prosperity as the result of war orders of one kind or another. That seems not to weigh in the balance at all; the whole desire seems to be to pass anything to some other government. However, that is not the fault of my hon. friend, and I shall be glad to look into this case. I know something of it myself, and if any way can be found out of the situation, I shall be glad to consult my hon. friend.

There is a matter I should like the minister to bring to the attention of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Gibson). I understand that like the army and the air force, when a man goes active in the Canadian navy he is automatically exempted from paying income tax. I presume this is done to recompense him for the dangers that he may encounter. I understand, however, that a man in the Canadian merchant marine is not granted this privilege, although the risks may be just as great as those faced by a man in the army. I have in mind an officer on one of the Imperial Oil tankers. I cannot imagine a more precarious job in this war at the present time than bringing oil from south America to Canadian ports. Surely this man is entitled to the same consideration as is given to men in the navy.

At the present time Canada has no marine corps,

War Appropriation-Naval Services
although practically every other country has found that such a corps is necessary. I believe it would add to Canada's naval prestige if we had such a corps, and I should like to know if the minister is going to do anything about it. The marine corps in the United States really acts as a commando corps. They also have a marine corps division of public relations in the United States which permits of the maximum cooperation between newspapers and the navy department. Has the minister anything to say in that regard?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: We have not considered a marine corps in this country.
We have no battleships.
There is not room for them on our warships.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: As my hon. friend knows, our navy started in a rather small way, with only 1,700 officers and men two and a half years ago. It is doubtful that we will feel it necessary to start the formation of a marine corps for some little time, but perhaps some day we may have such a corps.

A young man from Peterborough joined up some months ago, and when the destroyer he was on was sunk, he was transferred to a British ship. The Westclox club in Peterborough sends out twice a month to all its members parcels containing cigarettes, pipes and other little things that will be appreciated by the men. But the cigarettes are always taken out of this man's parcel. He gets the pipes and whatever else they send him, but the cigarettes are not there. This man is paid by the Canadian navy.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Who takes them out?
I do not know, and they want to know. The Western Clock people send these parcels to all men who have enlisted from their plants. Will the minister look into this?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
It is a large order. I shall find out from my hon. friend the name of the man and what ship he is serving on and endeavour to do something about it. It may be due to some rogueiy on the part of those handling the parcels; I suppose cigarettes are quite precious in certain parts of the world just now. If my hon. friend will give me the name of the ship and the name of the man I shall see what I can do. The Postmaster General (Mr. IMr. Fraser (Peterborough).]
Mulock) would probably be the proper person to handle this.

When a Canadian joins the imperial army in England he cannot get cigarettes, but in that case he is paid by the British government. This man is paid by the Canadian government, so that his case is slightly different.
It has been suggested to me that perhaps the navy could take a great number of the men who are rejected by the army because of flat feet. In the navy it does not matter, but in the army I know it does.
Can you walk on the water?
They do not use their feet on the water. If they cannot be taken on in the navy, can they be taken on in the merchant marine?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is a medical question. I should not like it to be understood that we are taking on those who have been rejected by the other services, but if there is some useful task that they can do, I know that we should be glad to consider them. As to the nierehant marine, there are some old skippers between sixty and sixty-five years of age at sea now who are a good deal over the army or navy age, but they are men of long experience on the sea. If these are the men to whom the hon. member refers, I think it would be considerably easier for them to get into the merchant marine, where the medical standard is not as strict as for the navy or army.

At
page 2265 of Hansard the minister said, in reference to a man who is missing:
If he is missing, his pay goes on for the rest of the month. I think that is the arrangement. When he is presumed killed his widow or dependent, as the ease may be, falls under the ordinary pension regulations.
If the man is a prisoner of war his pay continues for six months and then the allowance to the wife or other dependent is stopped. I know it is so in the air force; is it so in the navy? If a man is not presumed dead for six months, the allowance is cut off for the full six months. Can the minister give any information on that?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I
can get that information for my hon. friend.

A question was asked
last week as to buildings that were being put up for the navy by the Department of Public Works over and above the $20,000,000 expenditure for buildings which the navy itself is putting up.

War Appropriation-War Services

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I
think I answered no to that question when it was asked last week. The $20,000,000 covers all the buildings that are being built l'or the navy this year. It does not matter who is putting them up, because we have to pay for them and provide for them in our estimates. The $20,000,000 is the total cost of the new buildings that we are asking for this year.

I have been asked questions from time to time which indicate that people do not understand why it is that the navy is setting up a naval college at Royal Roads after thirty-two months of war when we have got along all this time with the present facilities and without such a college. And where is the navy going to get competent instructors and other personnel for this college? Can the minister enlighten me so that I in turn may enlighten those who ask me?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
That comment has been made about every new undertaking since the beginning of time. You would never start a new college or institution of any kind if you paid' attention to comments of that sort. If we had not started a naval college I think there would have been a great deal more criticism. We would have had people saying: Why are you not doing something to get ready? It is true that for the purposes of the war, assuming it will be over in two or three years, we could get along without a naval college. The naval college will not begin to turn out students until 1943, and then it will begin to turn out fifty or sixty young men a year. In the meantime, hundreds of young officers will have been trained through the shorter four months' training courses. But I do not think there is anyone in this country who will deny that we need such an institution. Four months is a short period within which to train a naval officer. The naval college will be a place to which a young man can go who wants to adopt the sea as a career. He will receive there two years of good solid training fitting him for permanent service in the navy or the merchant marine. I do not think any Canadian who looks at the problems which this country will have to face at the end of the war will challenge the wisdom of establishing such an institution.
Where are we going to get the instructors? That is a question that seems to be based on very little thought. We have as head of the college Kenneth Ketchum, the former principal of St. Andrew's college. Is there in all of Canada a man who enjoys a higher reputation in the teaching of boys and young
men? I do not think there is. He is well known, I am sure, to my hon. friends from the Toronto area, and indeed to many people throughout Canada. He is to head the academic staff of the college. He will have with him some men who were formerly at the Royal Military college, which, as hon. members know, has been closed for the duration so far as its ordinary purposes are concerned. Three or four of its instructors are going to assist us temporarily in the foundation of the naval college. We shall also have some naval officers, Captain Grant and several others of experience.
Is he to be the commandant?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes, he will have charge of discipline and the like, and Kenneth Ketchum will be in charge of the academic instruction. There is no dearth of available men to man the college, and man it well. I am sure it will be a credit to this country.
Is the Wasser-mann test given to young men who want to join the navy?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: We probably do what the other two services do. Is it given in the army?
It is optional in the army, I understand.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I will find out about that.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. T. THORSON (Minister of National War Services):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it was intended that I should follow the Minister of Munitions and Supply but it was impossible for him to be here this afternoon. In order, therefore, to save the time of the house and of the committee 1 shall commence with my statement.
With the permission of the committee I should like to make a general statement with regard to the national war services regulations, their operation, their results, the main amendments that have been made since last I addressed the committee on this subject, and then give some comments on criticisms that have been made. That general statement might then serve as the basis for questions from members of the committee.
Last November I gave a brief resume of the procedure that is laid down under the regulations from the time that the Department of National Defence sends its requisition to the Department of National War Services and the man who is called up reports to the training

War Appropriation-War Services
centre. I do not think it necessary to review that procedure again. Roughly, the relationship between the Department of National Defence and the Department of National War Services is that the Department of National Defence sends a monthly requisition to the Department of National War Services. The nature of that requisition was explained to the committee by the Minister of National Defence on May 4. The requisition states the number of men required to report to the training centre; it gives the total number of men required for the month. The detail of how that requirement is broken up is contained in a schedule attached to the requisition. It is indicated, for example, how many men are to report to the various training centres across the country. The requisition not only gives the total number of men required for the particular month and the date on which the men are required to report, but it also breaks down the requisition into the various training centres and administrative divisions.
Which department decides what age the men are to be?

The matter of age is
settled by a proclamation which is issued under the provisions of the national war service regulations.
That is a matter of government policy.

It is a matter of government policy from time to time. A proclamation is issued. The most recent one called men up who were bom in the years from 1912-1922, I believe. Then it is the duty of the Department of National War Services to comply with the requisition which comes from the Department of National Defence and to call men up for training in accordance with the requisition.
By mail?
We send out notices to the men in the various administrative divisions.

That is,
the notice is sent out by the divisional registrar?

It is sent out by the
divisional registrar. We operate the regulations through thirteen administrative divisions. In general these administrative divisions coincide in geographical outline with the military districts. There are two exceptions in that regard. Each one of these administrative divisions is headed by a board which consists of three persons. The chairman of the board is a judge of the superior court or other court of 
the province in which the greater portion of the administrative division is located, and there are two other members of the board. There is also a divisional registrar, who is the administrative officer of the division. In addition to the members of the board there are four persons who have a right to be present at hearings of the board and to make representations to it. These persons are respectively, a representative of the Department of National Defence, of the national war labour board, of agriculture, and of the director of national selective service. These four representatives are not actually members of the board, but they have the right to be present at all hearings and to make whatever representations they deem fit.
What is the basis on which the representative of agriculture is selected? Is he chosen from among the farmers?

The desire is to find a
person who thoroughly understands the agricultural situation in the administrative division and will see that those interests are safeguarded as far as possible.

Well, he
is named by the minister.

He is named by the
minister.
Certainly. He represents the minister.

And they act only when
an appeal is being made to the board?

They appear before the
board when the board hears applications for postponements.

On whose advice
does the minister name the representative of agriculture? Does he listen to any of the agricultural organizations?
Yes, he listens to them.
Does he pay any attention to them?	.

That, generally, is the
relationship between the Department of National Defence and the Department of National War Services.
Who is the representative of the department of agriculture in the province of New Brunswick?
Mr. T. Allen Best. He is a farmer and returned soldier of Stanley, in York county, New Brunswick.

Is there a man by the name of Barker on that list?

War Appropriation-War Services
No.
Best is the man?
Best is the representative of agriculture.

Who is the representative
for Saskatchewan?

Would the minister give
the names of the representatives of the prairie districts?

As yet only five representatives of agriculture have been appointed. If it is desired that I shall put their names on the record, I shall be glad to do so: administrative division E, with headquarters at Montreal, Anatole Gascon, a farmer of St. Frangois de Salle, Quebec; administrative division F, with headquarters at Quebec, Mr. J. A. DeBlois, insurance broker, of Beauce-ville East.
I have given the name of the representative of agriculture in New Brunswick. Then for administrative division I with headquarters at Charlottetown, P.E.I., Mr. Gordon Holmes, who is a barrister located at Charlottetown. For division N, headquarters at Edmonton, Mr. Walter Bissell, a farmer of Viking, Alberta.
When will appointees be selected for the other provinces-Manitoba for instance?

I cannot say when the other appointments will be made. Representations are being made from time to time. The matter is perhaps not quite as important now as it was prior to March 23, when the new regulations relating to persons wholly or mainly employed in agriculture came into effect. But consideration is being given to the subject.
Did the minister consult the provinces?
In some cases yes. There is no fixed procedure in regard to the matter.
Have all the representatives of labour been appointed?
I think they have, but I am not sure about that. They are not appointed by the Minister of National War Services, of course; they are representatives of the national war labour board.
What control if any has the minister over the several national service boards in the various provinces with a view to securing uniformity of interpretation and application of the regulations?

I pointed out that the divisions are presided over by a board the
chairman of which is a judge. The decisions of the boards on applications for postponement are final. Ottawa, April 17, 1942. Press Release by Hon. J. T. Thorson, Minister of National War Services.
There still appears to be some misunderstanding of the effect of the national war services regulations, 1940 (recruits) as amended by order in council P.C. 2252, dated March 21, 1942, and their application to persons who are "wholly or mainly employed in agriculture".
The national war services regulations, 1940 (recruits), govern the subject of calling up men for compulsory military training. They were amended by order in council P.C. 2252 in order to give effect to a fundamental alteration in government policy as laid down by the "stabilization of employment in agriculture regulations, 1942", enacted by order in council P.C. 2251, dated March 21, 1942.
The national war services regulations are administered by thirteen administrative division boards, each board consisting of three members, of which the chairman is a judge of a superior or other court of the province in which the larger part of the administrative division is situated.
The amendments to the national war services regulations contained in P.C. 2252 apply only to the persons who are covered by the term "person wholly or mainly employed in agriculture". The term "person wholly or mainly employed in agriculture" is specially defined in the amended regulations. The term applies only to the following two classes of persons; it means
(1)	any person, who on the 23rd day of March, 1942, was wholly or mainly employed or engaged in agriculture, and it includes [Mr. Thorson.j
(2)	any person, rvho on the said 23rd day of March, 1942, was employed or engaged, but only seasonally, in a primary industry, but whose last employment or occupation immediately prior to such seasonal employment or engagement in a primary industry was wholly or mainly in agriculture.
For the purposes of the amended regulations, the term "agriculture" means the production of field crops, fruits, vegetables, honey, poultry, eggs, live stock, milk, butter or cheese, and the term "primary industry" means and includes lumbering and logging, forestry, fishing and trapping.
The amended regulations do not apply to any other classes of persons. They do not apply to any persons, who, prior to March 23, were engaged in activities other than agriculture or seasonal primary industries, as defined in the amended regulations. Consequently', any persons who left their occupations after March 23, 1942, with a view to returning to or engaging in agriculture in order to obtain postponements of military training until further notice will not be able to do so. All such persons are still subject to the national war services regulations as they stood before the recent amendments. Such persons may still make applications for postponement of their military training, but such applications for postponement will be dealt with by the divisional boards in the same manner and subject to the same principles as heretofore.
The procedure for administering the national war services regulations, as amended, may be briefly summarized, so far as they relate to the classes of persons covered by the amended regulations, as follows:
(1)	"Notices-medical examination" under section 12 of the regulations will be sent out by the divisional registrars in exactly the same manner as heretofore. There will be no change in this procedure.
These notices must not be disregarded. Failure to comply with the requirements of the notices, namely, to report for medical examination, will render the person guilty of such failure, liable to the penalties imposed by law.
(2)	On receipt of the "Notice-medical examination" the person to whom the notice is addressed may, if he wishes to do so, apply for a postponement order,' but he must do so in writing to the divisional registrar who sent him the notice within eight clear days of the date appearing on the notice.
(3)	If the person who receives the notice is a "person wholly or mainly employed in agriculture" as defined in the amended regulations, he may apply for a postponement order on the ground that he is a person wholly or mainly-employed in agriculture within the meaning of the amended regulations. He need not assign any other ground for his application.
(4)	The application will then be dealt with by the divisional board as it deals with other applications for postponements.
There, is, however, this fundamental difference, namely, _ that if the applicant is a person wholly or mainly employed in agriculture within the meaning of the amended regulations, the board, subject to certain exceptions hereafter mentioned, shall grant him a postponement order until further notice and such postponement order shall be an allocation of such person to agriculture.

It is this direction to the board, namely, that the board shall grant him a postponement order until further notice, that constitutes the "fundamental alteration of the policy regarding compulsory military training and service where such service touches persons wholly or mainly employed in agriculture," referred to by the Prime Minister in his speech in the House of Commons on Tuesday, March 24, 1942.
Previously, under subsections (1) and (2) of section 14 of the National war services regulations, it was provided that the board "shall have power to grant an advancement or postponement order when it is of the opinion that it is in the national interest to do so," but there was no obligation upon the board to grant such orders. The matter was left to the discretion of the boards.
It was also provided that "no postponement order may be made for more than six months, but, upon reviewing the application, the board may grant one or more extensions." It was also provided that in respect of certain' applications for postponement, such as by a man engaged in farming, fishing, lumbering, trapping, etc., "the board shall take into account the supply of labour available and the importance of the particular applicant's occupation to the national economy."
There has therefore been a fundamental change of base in the regulations. It is not a question of greater latitude having been given to the boards in the matter of granting postponement orders. Nor is it a matter of preferential treatment. The amendments go much further and constitute a fundamental change of approach, both by the applicant and by the board. When the applicant has shown that he is a person wholly or mainly employed or engaged in agriculture within the meaning of the amended regulations, he is prima facie entitled 'to a postponement order until further notice. He does not have to prove, as was the ease formerly, a special case for postponement of a fixed duration.
The fundamental change in the character of the amended regulations may be stated as follows. Under the regulations as they stood prior to the amendments, the applicant had to make out a special case for postponement. The granting of a postponement order was within the discretion of the board and the postponement order was ohly for a fixed period of time. The applicant was still regarded as being a person primarly required for compulsory military training wrhen his period of postponement was concluded. Under the amended regulations the situation is entirely changed. When the applicant has shown that he is a person wholly or mainly employed in agriculture within the meaning of the amended regulations, it is mandatory upon the board, subject to the ex' ceptions hereinafter mentioned, to grant the postponement order. Furthermore, the postponement order is until further notice and it constitutes an allocation of the applicant to agriculture rather than to military service.
Precautions have been taken against abuse of the regulations and their undue extension to persons not intended to be covered by them. The board is not required -to grant a postponement order until further notice to an applicant if it is established to the satisfaction of the board, either (1) that the applicant is not an essential worker in agriculture, or (2) that -the applicant has at -any time subsequent to March 23 ceased to be actually employed or engaged in agriculture or in -a primary industry. The
onus of proof in each of these cases is not upon the applicant. These safeguards against the undue extension of -the amended regulations to persons not intended to be covered by them are within the exclusive jurisdiction of the divisional boards.
' Where a person is wholly or mainly employed in agriculture within the meaning of the amended regulations and has been granted a postponement order until further notice, there is an allocation of such person to agriculture.
The effect of the amended regulations will therefore be as stated by the Prime Minister in the House of Commons on Tuesday, March 24, 1942, "Under new regulations, farmers, farmers' sons and agricultural labourers will normally not be obliged to undertake compulsory military training and service."
At hearings of the boards, representatives of the Department of National Defence, of the national war labour board, of agriculture and of the director of national selective service are entitled to be present and -to make such representations as they may deem fit. Their presence and -their right to make representations to the boards are intended as guarantees that all interests connected with the war effort and the manpower requirements for the war effort in each aspect of it will be safeguarded.
The divisional boards have since their inception dealt in a judicial and sympathetic manner with applications for postponement made by farmers and other persons engaged in essential activities. In some agricultural areas of Canada, particularly areas close to large cities with large concentrations of war industries, the agricultural situation was becoming serious as the result of a number of causes, such as a large flow of agricultural labour into war industry, extensive voluntary enlistments with the armed forces, and. to a lesser degree, the calling of men for military training, and the ability of the country to carry out its agricultural commitments in the matter of essential food production was being threatened. It was therefore necessary to enact the "stabilization of employment in agriculture regulations, 1942." The essential purpose of these regulations is to prevent the agricultural situation in Canada from deteriorating beyond its present position and to enable the country to carry out the important food production aspect of its war effort.
The purpose and objective of these regulations and of the amendments to the national war services regulations were stated by the Prime Minister in the House of Commons on Tuesday, March 24, 1942, in the following terms:-
The policy of stabilizing employment in agriculture represents what, in effect, is a block allocation to agriculture of the persons best fitted for food production. It constitutes a form of large scale selection for national service which should go far to ensure the supply of manpower essential to the food production aspect of the national war effort. Care has been taken to provide against abuses of postponement orders until further notice. A person who has been granted such a postponement order and has thus been allocated to agriculture may lose the right to such postponement and allocation if he ceases to be actually employed or engaged in agriculture or in a primary industry and such fact is brought to the attention of the board by any of the representatives above referred to.

large across the country, Canada, from the point of view of its agricultural commitments as part of its war effort, could fill those commitments provided there was not any further undue strain on the ranks of agriculture. When a man who has been called up under the national war service regulations reports to the training centre he is out of the jurisdiction of the Department of National War Services and is subject to the jurisdiction of the Department of National Defence. On March 12 of this year order in council P.C. 1916 was passed, by way of amendment to the reserve army (special) regulations of 1941. Under section 23 of these regulations as amended, provision is made for an application for leave being made by the R recruit, as he is termed. He makes that application to his commanding officer, in writing, showing the reasons and facts upon which it is based,

together with statements corroborating the facts made by statutory declaration or attestation under oath. The commanding officer forwards the recommendation to the district officer commanding. The district officer commanding may forward the application, with whatever recommendation or representation he may see fit, to the appropriate national war services board. It is not obligatory upon the district officer commanding to forward the application for leave to the national war services board. The reason for not making it mandatory for the district officer commanding to forward the application is to discourage frivolous applications. I think hon. members can rest assured that every bona fide application, every application with merit in it, will be referred by the district officer commanding to the national war services board.
The reason why this arrangement was arrived at was, in the main, to secure uniformity of treatment in dealing with applications for leave coming from, persons who were soldiers by reason of the fact that they had reported to a training centre and were subject to the jurisdiction of the Department of National Defence. In the regulation that I have cited, No. 23 of the reserve army (special) regulations of 1941, referred to in order in council P.C. 1916, it is provided that leave may be granted upon such circumstances, reasons or grounds being established as would have entitled the applicant when called out ab initio to postponement before the commencement of his training. The idea was that the district officer commanding would forward these applications for leave to the national war services board, and the national war services board would deal with these applications for leave upon the same circumstances, reasons and grounds as would govern the board in dealing with an application for postponement of military training. That was the purpose, to get uniformity.
The boards hear these applications. They may investigate the case and, after a review or rehearing thereof, may make recommendations to the district officer commanding. On receiving a recommendation of the board the district officer commanding will grant leave for the period recommended by the board. It is mandatory upon the district officer commanding to grant the leave in accordance with the recommendation of the board. That, of course, is subject to the exigencies of the military situation, which might require that that leave be curtailed or refused. Apart from that, the recommendation made by the board is binding upon the military authorities.
